notes.meaning: The Lord commands Moses to speak directly to Aaron, his sons, and the entire nation of Israel. Worship and sacrifice were not private matters left only to the priests, but concerned every family. God's rules for holy living applied to the whole community together.

God commanded that domestic animals like cattle, sheep, or goats could not be slaughtered out in the fields or camp away from the sanctuary. Anyone who killed such an animal without presenting it at the Tent of Meeting was counted guilty of shedding blood, as if he were a murderer, and had to be cut off from the people. This rule kept the Israelites from setting up private altars and falling into pagan practices.

Before this law was given, the people often slaughtered animals in the open fields where idol worship easily took root. God ordered them to bring these animals to the priest at the sanctuary to be offered as peace offerings. A peace offering was a shared sacred meal where a portion was given to God on the altar and the rest was enjoyed with family in fellowship with Him.

The priest caught the blood of the animal and sprinkled it against the altar of burnt offering, then burned the fat on the fire. In the sacrificial laws, the fat was viewed as the richest and best part of the animal, reserved for God alone as a pleasing aroma. This showed that God owned the life of the animal and received the very best portion.

God warned Israel to stop offering sacrifices to goat demons, false deities that people had learned to worship in Egypt. The Lord describes idol worship as prostitution or adultery because Israel had entered into a marriage-like covenant with Him and had broken faith. Serving God alone was meant to shield His people from dangerous and corrupt rituals.

This rule applied equally to native Israelites and to foreigners living among them. Anyone who brought a burnt offering or sacrifice anywhere other than the entrance of the Tent of Meeting was cut off from the community. God required everyone in the camp to worship in the single, unified way He had revealed.

God issued a strict ban against eating blood, whether done by an Israelite or a resident foreigner. If anyone broke this law, God Himself promised to oppose that person and cut them off from the people. Even if a person ate blood secretly where human judges could not see, God declared that He would personally bring judgment.

The reason for this rule is that the physical life of every living creature is carried in its blood. God appointed blood on the altar to make atonement, which means providing a way to cover sin and reconcile people to God by accepting the life of an innocent animal in place of the sinner. Because blood was set apart for this holy purpose of redemption, it was never to be treated as common food.

Because blood belongs to the altar for atonement, God commanded that no Israelite and no foreigner living among them could eat it. The repeated command reminded the entire nation that God's gift of life must be held sacred. Keeping this rule helped maintain reverence for God's way of forgiveness.

When a hunter caught a wild animal or bird that was permitted for food, he could not offer it on the altar, but he still had to respect its life. He was required to drain out its blood and cover it with dirt. This act served as a kind of burial for the blood, showing reverence to God as the creator and giver of life.

God emphasizes once more that the blood is the very life of all living creatures, and anyone who consumes it must be cut off. Repeating the instruction drove home how essential it was to treat life with dignity and obedience. It also prevented Israel from copying pagan cultures that consumed blood during hunting or religious rites.

An animal that died on its own or was killed by a wild predator still held undrained blood within its body, making it unfit to eat. If an Israelite or a convert ate such meat by mistake, he became ceremonially unclean and had to wash his clothes and bathe in water until evening. If he refused or ignored this cleansing, he remained guilty and had to bear the penalty of his disobedience.
